turns.en: Yeah. So, acronym PULL, there's a P — project. They have a project on their to-do list. You can think of a project like a job to be done. Um, you know, Bob Moesta, you've had him on. turns.en: That unavoidable piece — I see why that is so important. And this is an example. Basically you need all four here.
turns.zh: 那个不可避免的部分——我明白为什么它如此重要。而这是一个例子。基本上你需要所有四个都在这里。

turns.en: Yes. So that's a good lesson here is all four need to exist for real PULL.
turns.zh: 是的。所以这里有一个很好的教训，就是所有四个都需要存在才是真正的 PULL。

turns.en: In the first example that to-do to me doesn't feel like it's like a to-do that just wrote down. It's kind of this general to-do just like generally save time. Is that an okay P for a project for to be able to do just a or is or is was this like specifically on every financial advisor's to-do list?
turns.zh: 在第一个例子中，那个待办事项对我来说感觉不像是随便写下的待办事项。它更像是一个一般的待办事项，就像一般性地节省时间。对于一个项目来说，仅仅是一个一般的待办事项可以吗？还是说这具体地在每个财务顾问的待办事项列表上？

turns.en: Yeah. So, it was a thing that I wouldn't say it's like actually something they wrote down on their to-do list, but it was like a thing they were doing all the time. It was a part of their workflow and while they were doing it, they were trying not to do it. Like I think there's like a — the action I'm doing right now on my calendar and then the project is my intention while I'm doing it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，这件事我不会说它实际上是他们写在待办事项列表上的东西，但它是他们一直在做的事情。这是他们工作流程的一部分，而当他们做这件事时，他们试图不做它。就像我认为有一个——我现在在日历上做的行动，然后项目是我在做这件事时的意图。

turns.en: And so while I'm doing it, the project on my mental to-do list was like spend the least amount of time doing this annoying thing.
turns.zh: 所以当我做这件事时，我心理待办清单上的项目就是：花最少的时间做这件烦人的事。

turns.en: Got it. And so if a founder or product team is listening to this and they're struggling with their product, it's probably one of these four is not there.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以如果创始人或产品团队在听这个节目，并且他们在产品上挣扎，那很可能是因为这四个要素中有一个缺失了。

turns.en: Yeah. You need all four at once. If you find P without U and in the L's, so you find something that somebody's trying to do kind of, but they're not actually trying to do it right now and their existing options aren't good enough, what they'll do is they'll complain and they won't buy. If they have P and U, but their L's are good enough, they're going to say, 'Yeah, that's exactly what we're doing right now and working with Claude Code on it. We're going to figure it out.'
turns.zh: 是的。你需要同时具备所有四个要素。如果你发现了 P 但没有 U 和 L，也就是说你发现某人在某种程度上试图做某事，但他们现在并没有真正在做，而且他们现有的选择还不够好，他们会做的是抱怨，而不会购买。如果他们有了 P 和 U，但他们的 L 已经足够好，他们会说：‘是的，那正是我们现在在做的，并且正在用 Claude Code 处理。我们会搞定的。’

turns.en: Something along these lines that you talk about is that this pull exists. It's like this thing that's already there and you're just kind of this like I don't know hunter looking for the pull and discovering it. Talk a bit about that.
turns.zh: 你谈到的一个类似的观点是，这种拉力是存在的。它就像已经存在的东西，而你就像是一个猎人，寻找并发现这种拉力。请谈谈这一点。

turns.en: Yeah, this was super liberating when I like realized this because I always thought that I was incompetent. I wasn't good at convincing the market to want my product. And it was from that perspective of okay, I'm building something that's really valuable and people aren't buying. How do I convince them to want it to buy? And it turns out this poll, this project on their to-do list exists before and independent of me, which means I just have to go out there and find it. I don't have to convince people to have pull. And it's like I haven't quite figured out how to do that, but I think it's very very hard to do if it's possible at all.
turns.zh: 是的，当我意识到这一点时，我感到非常解放，因为我总以为自己无能。我不擅长说服市场想要我的产品。那是从这样一个角度出发的：好吧，我在构建一些非常有价值的东西，但人们不买。我如何说服他们想要购买？而事实证明，这种拉力，他们待办清单上的这个项目，在我之前并且独立于我存在，这意味着我只需要走出去找到它。我不需要说服人们拥有拉力。就像我还没完全弄清楚如何做到那样，但我认为即使可能，也非常非常困难。

turns.en: That feels very familiar just trying to convince people. Look, this is so great. It's going to solve so many of your problems. Uh, and I love these idea this like I just love how very specific and concrete it makes all of these general pieces of advice around finding product market fit, coming up with ideas. It just tells you exactly here's what it looks like. Um, something else you talk about, you mentioned this earlier, this idea that it it needs to feel weird for them not to buy it. That's like the sign that this is right, that it's like it's weird. Why aren't you buying this? Talk a bit about that.
turns.zh: 那种试图说服别人的感觉非常熟悉。看，这太棒了。它会解决你的很多问题。嗯，我喜欢这个想法，我就是喜欢它如何让所有这些关于找到产品市场契合、提出想法的通用建议变得非常具体和实在。它直接告诉你这就是它看起来的样子。嗯，你还谈到了另一点，你之前提到过，这个想法是，如果他们不买，会感觉很奇怪。这就像是正确的标志，就像很奇怪。你为什么不买这个？请谈谈这一点。

turns.en: Most people most of the time are like fine. It would be weird if they bought our product given what's on their to-do list, given what they have, given their options, like so it'd be weird if they bought. But a person with pull is weird not to buy. They should actually pull the product out of your hands because they are like that coiled spring. And so if you talk to somebody who has pull, the conversation should basically go like, 'Wait a second, you can do what? Okay, how do we get started? Does the product exist yet? Like how do how do we get on board?' where basically every other conversation you have with somebody who doesn't have pull can have anything other than that. They can be enthusiastic and nice and say, 'Wow, that's amazing. That's super interesting. That's totally the future of our industry. Wow, I can see how that would save us so much money,' but they're not saying, 'I need this right now.' And that's how you know they actually have pull.
turns.zh: 大多数人在大多数时候都还好。考虑到他们的待办清单、他们拥有的东西、他们的选择，如果他们买了我们的产品，那才会奇怪。所以如果他们买了，那才奇怪。但一个有拉力的人不买才奇怪。他们实际上应该把产品从你手中抢走，因为他们就像那个紧绷的弹簧。所以如果你和一个有拉力的人交谈，对话基本上应该是这样的：‘等等，你能做什么？好的，我们怎么开始？产品已经存在了吗？我们怎么加入？’而基本上你与没有拉力的人的其他所有对话都可以是任何其他内容。他们可以热情友好地说：‘哇，太棒了。那超级有趣。那完全是我们行业的未来。哇，我能看出那会为我们节省很多钱’，但他们不会说：‘我现在就需要这个。’这就是你如何知道他们确实有拉力。

turns.en: Those conversations sound very familiar. Okay. So before we get into the kind of the whole journey of the startup process and how you can use this framework in that journey, anything else around just the general idea of the pull framework that's important to share?
turns.zh: 那些对话听起来非常熟悉。好的。那么在我们进入创业过程的整个旅程以及你如何在这个旅程中使用这个框架之前，关于拉力框架的一般概念，还有什么重要的要分享吗？

turns.en: One of the main mistakes people make is thinking that pull is a thing that a company has. It's a thing a person has. Even if you're selling enterprise software, you're selling not to the company. You're not selling to SpaceX. You're selling to just going to your genable conversation. you're selling to like the head of legal at SpaceX who has a project on her to-do list that that they can't do themselves.
turns.zh: 人们犯的主要错误之一是认为拉力是公司拥有的东西。它是个人拥有的东西。即使你销售企业软件，你也不是在向公司销售。你不是在向 SpaceX 销售。你是在向 SpaceX 的法务主管销售，她的待办清单上有一个她自己无法完成的项目。

turns.en: That is really useful. So, it's not like SpaceX needs this. It's like say Jen needs this. Uh and you're saying that that's often a mistake people make. They don't think about the specific person with this need.
turns.zh: 这真的很有用。所以，不是 SpaceX 需要这个，而是比如 Jen 需要这个。嗯，你说这是人们常犯的错误。他们没有考虑到有这种需求的具体个人。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. It's it's super common to say we sell to right like mid-market private equity companies. It's like you don't you sell to a partner or an operating partner in there who's specifically trying to do X, Y, and Z.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。非常常见的是说我们销售给中型私募股权公司。这就像你不是向公司销售，而是向其中的一个合伙人或运营合伙人销售，他们具体试图做 X、Y 和 Z。

turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So, through the lens of this framework, let's go through kind of the key moments of an early stage startup, finding product market fit. So, I want to talk about coming up with an idea, getting your first sales call, closing your first deal, and then kind of scaling from there. So, let's start with coming up with an idea. How how can people use this framework to help them come up with ideas that are more likely to actually be successful?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。那么，通过这个框架的视角，让我们梳理一下早期初创公司的关键时刻，找到产品市场契合。所以，我想谈谈提出想法、获得第一个销售电话、完成第一笔交易，然后从那里扩展。那么，让我们从提出想法开始。人们如何利用这个框架来帮助他们提出更有可能成功的想法？

turns.en: As a founder, I I have a notebook of ideas that are all like, 'What if we built an API for APIs kind of thing like they're there all these like product ideas and the product ideas all sound unhinged?' And so I can never tell between product ideas, what's a good idea and what's a bad idea. Well, fortunately, the pull framework is a is a thing that is upstream of your product idea that says, I believe there is a person who is trying to do X right now. We who basically weird not to buy. And so, what I found to be helpful is to use the pull framework to stake out a claim and say, I believe for whatever idea I have, I believe this specific person is stuck. And so I'm going to go and talk to them and see do they want to do they try to buy from me even before we have a product. And so for me the the idea of the the um the poll framework is is to come up with a hypothesis of who has pull and then go and test that.
turns.zh: 作为创始人，我有一个想法笔记本，上面都是类似‘如果我们为 API 构建一个 API 之类的’这样的产品想法，这些产品想法听起来都很疯狂。所以我永远分不清产品想法中哪个是好主意，哪个是坏主意。幸运的是，拉力框架是位于你产品想法上游的东西，它说，我相信现在有一个人正试图做 X。我们基本上不买才奇怪。所以，我发现有帮助的是使用拉力框架来明确主张，说，我相信无论我有什么想法，我相信这个特定的人被卡住了。所以我要去和他们谈谈，看看他们是否想——甚至在我们有产品之前就尝试从我这里购买。所以对我来说，拉力框架的想法是提出谁有拉力的假设，然后去测试它。

turns.en: And then the question becomes okay how do you find this pole idea this pole hypothesis what do you do for that?
turns.zh: 那么问题就变成了：好的，你如何找到这个拉力想法、这个拉力假设，你为此做什么？

turns.en: I have some fairly strong opinions on this. Like I don't think we take this stage seriously enough. Like if your life depended on it, how would would you would you be doing like 10 customer interviews for like 30 minutes on Zoom? No. You would go all out. You would go in person. And I have like a couple stories of friends who have done crazy things to go and like do the job with the potential customer to feel it firsthand to find that pull firsthand and they've either built something that they would buy themselves or they've like embedded with people to find that like that moment when someone will is like trying to do something and stuck.
turns.zh: 我对此有相当强烈的看法。就像我认为我们没有足够认真地对待这个阶段。就像如果你的生命取决于它，你会怎么做？你会做 10 个 30 分钟的 Zoom 客户访谈吗？不。你会全力以赴。你会亲自去。我有几个朋友的故事，他们做了疯狂的事情，去和潜在客户一起做工作，亲身感受，亲身找到那种拉力，他们要么构建了自己会买的东西，要么嵌入到人们中去发现那个时刻，当某人试图做某事并被卡住时。

turns.en: Amazing. Uh so the advice here is don't sit around and brainstorm. Don't uh just look for big markets and figure out where there might be something massive.
turns.zh: 太棒了。嗯，所以这里的建议是不要坐着头脑风暴。不要只是寻找大市场并找出可能有什么巨大的东西。

ts.sec: Finding real problems through firsthand experience

turns.en: What you're saying here is almost like this lens of if your life depended on it, how would you find a problem that is likely to be real, I guess have real pull? And what I'm hearing here is get in the weeds, get your hands dirty, get in the way. This reminds me of a quote from Naan, who is the head of product at Linear now—he just went to OpenAI—describing what he looks for when he's trying to find opportunities. He describes: I want to feel the pain of the person the same way they feel the pain.
turns.zh: 你这里说的几乎就像这样一个视角：如果你的生命取决于它，你会如何找到一个很可能是真实的问题，我想是有真正拉动力的问题？而我在这里听到的是深入细节、亲自动手、参与进去。这让我想起 Naan 的一句话，他现在是 Linear 的产品负责人——他刚去了 OpenAI——描述他在寻找机会时看重什么。他描述说：我想像那个人感受痛苦一样去感受他们的痛苦。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.en: And what you're saying is the way to do that is get in there with people building the thing. Is there an example of doing that?
turns.zh: 而你说的方法是跟正在构建这个东西的人一起深入进去。有没有这样做的例子？

turns.en: Yeah. So, a friend from school, he had no idea what he wanted to build. He had no product idea. He wasn't—he didn't have my notebook. He didn't have any of that. He just said, you know, I like serving small businesses. I like small business. I'd like to just find somebody I like to serve and I'll figure out the idea from that. And so he wrote out a list of industries that he thought might be interesting. And then he went and shadowed them and worked with them for days at a time. And so he started with solar panel installers and he hated them and they hated him. So he moved on to the next one. He eventually worked his way to independent physical therapists and he went and spent days with them. He loved them. They loved him. And it was like okay cool. What is the pull here? What should I do? And so he watched over their shoulder days on end. He even tried to buy a physical therapy franchise to be able to see the P&L and was actually considering it. And in that process, he came up with something like, wait a second, it looks like you're trying to do X and are stuck there. And so it's firsthand experience is what you should do there.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，一个学校的朋友，他完全不知道想构建什么。他没有产品想法。他没有我的笔记本。他什么都没有。他只是说，你知道，我喜欢服务小企业。我喜欢小企业。我想找到一个我喜欢服务的人，然后从中想出点子。于是他写了一个他认为可能有趣的行业列表。然后他去跟踪他们，和他们一起工作，一干就是好几天。他从太阳能电池板安装商开始，他讨厌他们，他们也讨厌他。所以他转向下一个。他最终找到了独立物理治疗师，他和他们待了几天。他喜欢他们。他们也喜欢他。然后就像，好吧酷。这里的拉动力是什么？我该做什么？于是他连续几天从他们肩膀上方观察。他甚至试图购买一家物理治疗加盟店，以便能看到损益表，并且实际上在考虑。在这个过程中，他想到了类似，等一下，看起来你在试图做 X 并卡在那里。所以是第一手经验，这就是你应该做的。

turns.en: Awesome. So like live it yourself and live it. And is the reason you need to do that—is it partly because people would have discovered it if it was easy? Basically somebody else would have found the idea. Why do you think that is so important, approaching it this way?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以就像自己亲身经历并体验。你需要这样做的原因——部分是因为如果容易的话别人早就发现了？基本上别人早就找到这个想法了。你为什么认为这样 approach 如此重要？

turns.en: Yeah, I'd say I'll give two reasons. One is, you know, these things don't really emerge from a whiteboard. Like it would be weird if his idea came to him that he eventually wound up finding from brainstorming. Think of how many different ideas he could have come up with. And it wasn't something that—it was something he saw only by observing, where it's unclear that that would have emerged in an interview either. But I say the second thing is more of a philosophical thing, which is you're building a company to serve this kind of person. The whole point of building a company is to serve somebody, to help them do something. And so if you don't have firsthand experience, how are you going to make the thousands of decisions it takes to actually build something that serves them?
turns.zh: 是的，我会给出两个原因。第一，你知道，这些东西并不是真的从白板上冒出来的。如果他最终找到的想法是从头脑风暴中得来的，那会很奇怪。想想他可能想出多少不同的想法。而且这不是——这是他只有通过观察才看到的东西，而通过访谈也不清楚是否会浮现。但我要说的第二点更偏向哲学，那就是你正在建立一家公司来服务这类人。建立公司的全部意义就是服务某人，帮助他们做某事。所以如果你没有第一手经验，你如何做出构建真正服务于他们的东西所需的成千上万个决定？

turns.en: And is the idea once you have this insight, say with this physical therapy company, you write it out through the pull framework to kind of pressure—is that what you call it, the pull hypothesis? Is that right?
turns.zh: 那么想法是，一旦你有了这个洞察，比如对这家物理治疗公司，你通过拉动力框架把它写出来，以施加压力——你是这么叫的吗，拉动力假设？对吗？

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: So talk about that just like say you have this insight and I'm curious what he actually found with his physical therapy business and how to kind of start to think about it through the pull framework.
turns.zh: 那就谈谈这个，就像假设你有了这个洞察，我很好奇他在物理治疗业务中实际发现了什么，以及如何开始通过拉动力框架来思考它。

turns.en: Yeah. So you then take that and say okay this is the kind of idea I believe this kind of person—this physical therapist—is trying to cut some specific cost on their P&L. I can't actually remember what it was, unavoidable for XYZ reasons. And their existing options of getting a consultant to come in and do this wasn't good enough for some specific reason: it was too expensive, it was too slow. Wrote out that pull hypothesis and then what he did next was super important, which was he said he showed it to that person, said, 'Is this you?' Person said, 'Oh my god, yeah, that's exactly the thing.' Said, 'Okay, great. Would you buy something if I helped you get this done?' 'Yeah, totally.' 'Okay, great.' And then he said, 'I need to go talk to five other physical therapists and just make sure this repeats.' And then he did that and they also pulled, which was the really important thing to make sure he wasn't just building a product for one person.
turns.zh: 是的。所以你接着拿这个说，好吧，这是我认为这类人——这位物理治疗师——试图削减损益表上某项特定成本的想法。我其实不记得具体是什么了，由于 XYZ 原因不可避免。而他们现有的请顾问来做这件事的选项由于某些具体原因不够好：太贵了，太慢了。写下那个拉动力假设，然后他接下来做的非常重要，就是他把这个展示给那个人，说：‘这是你吗？’那人说：‘天哪，是的，正是这样。’他说：‘好的，太好了。如果我帮你完成这个，你会买吗？’‘是的，当然。’‘好的，太好了。’然后他说：‘我需要去和其他五位物理治疗师谈谈，确保这个会重复。’然后他这么做了，他们也拉了，这是非常重要的一点，确保他不是只为一两个人构建产品。

turns.en: What is it that he showed these companies? Is it the four bullet points with here's the project, here's why it's unavoidable, or is it something else?
turns.zh: 他给这些公司展示的是什么？是四个要点，包括这是项目、这是为什么不可避免，还是别的什么？

turns.en: Yeah. So I actually like recommend having two slides. One slide is basically the pull framework. You don't have to show them the pull framework because no one's going to understand it. You can just say, 'Here's what I hear: you're trying to do X right now because of Y, and you've considered this but it's not good enough for this reason.' You say, 'Do I have that roughly right?' And then the second slide is a kind of conceptual overview of how I can help. So it sounds like you're looking for a way to cut this line item that's faster than a consultant. We could offer that for XYZ. Does that kind of fit what you're looking for? And you're looking for the first slide for them to say, 'Oh my god, yes.' And the second slide, 'Yeah, how does it work? How exactly, you know, how do we move forward?'
turns.zh: 是的。所以我实际上建议准备两页幻灯片。第一页基本上是拉动力框架。你不必给他们看拉动力框架，因为没人会理解。你只需说：‘这是我听到的：你现在正试图做 X，因为 Y，你考虑过这个，但由于这个原因不够好。’你说：‘我大致说对了吗？’然后第二页是我如何帮助的概念性概述。所以听起来你在寻找一种比顾问更快地削减这个项目的方法。我们可以提供 XYZ。这符合你在寻找的吗？你希望第一页让他们说：‘天哪，是的。’第二页说：‘是的，怎么运作？具体如何，你知道，我们如何推进？’

turns.en: What I love about your stuff is it's very plug-and-play, pragmatic. So we'll actually show a slide of the actual template you have people use to fill this out. So the phrasing, I'll read it from this slide too: There's a project on your to-do list and it's unavoidable right now because of this, and options you looked into are this and they're lacking for this reason. Amazing. I love this. So the idea is you have this little slide that you just create and run by people, and the idea is this is the hypothesis. And what does it look like when there's pull once you show it to them? Is it like they're ready to send you money? Is it their pupils dilate? What do you look for?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你的东西的地方是它非常即插即用、务实。所以我们将实际展示一页你让人们用来填写的模板。所以措辞，我也从这页幻灯片上读一下：你的待办清单上有一个项目，由于这个原因现在不可避免，你研究过的选项是这个，但由于这个原因它们有欠缺。太棒了。我喜欢这个。所以想法是你有这个小幻灯片，你创建它并让人们过目，想法是这是假设。那么一旦你展示给他们，当有拉动力时是什么样子？是他们准备给你打钱吗？是他们的瞳孔放大吗？你看什么？

turns.en: Yeah, you look for a couple things. The thing that really really matters is that they actually try to buy. They say, 'Okay, cool. How do we get started?' And they will do that.
turns.zh: 是的，你看几件事。真正重要的是他们实际上试图购买。他们说：‘好的，酷。我们怎么开始？’而他们会这么做。

turns.en: I have a friend who was selling into pharma. He pivoted around for a while, but he knew he found pull when an exec in pharma, before he had a product, said, 'If you can do that, I will pay you right now.' So that's the signal you are looking for. What you're looking for is them leaning in: 'Wait a second, you can do what?' What you're not looking for is kind of leaned-out enthusiasm: 'Oh, well, tell me more. Well, let me—yeah, we'll think about it. Could you send more information so our team can review that?' Any of those kinds of things. Anything that is not like, 'Okay, how do we actually move forward on this?' is just not worth your life force going after.
turns.zh: 我有一个朋友，他做医药行业的销售。他摸索了一段时间，但当他找到“拉力”时，他知道了——那是在他还没有产品的时候，一位医药行业的高管对他说：“如果你能做到，我现在就付钱给你。”所以这就是你要找的信号。你要找的是他们主动靠近：“等等，你能做这个？”你要找的不是那种敷衍的热情：“哦，好吧，再多告诉我一些。嗯，让我们——好的，我们会考虑的。你能发更多信息给我们团队评估一下吗？”诸如此类。任何不是“好的，我们怎么实际推进这件事？”的反应，都不值得你投入精力去追。

turns.en: It's interesting how much body language and just the physical experience of getting excited about an idea is a sign that it is good. I just had Josh Woodward on the podcast, head of Google Labs, and he's similarly like you see a twinkle in their eyes and their eyes just light up. And it's so interesting that that's a sign of pull.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，身体语言和对一个想法感到兴奋的生理体验，很大程度上是它很好的标志。我刚请了 Google Labs 负责人 Josh Woodward 上播客，他也类似地说，你看到他们眼里有光，眼睛就亮了。有趣的是，那就是“拉力”的标志。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.en: Yeah. Is what you're seeing is—is it weird for them not to buy right now? Are they behaving as if it's weird for them not to buy? Is there like a—you know, there's like the 'I will buy this idea' like they say they will buy it versus a sign they will actually buy it. Is it the body language? Like how do you know they're serious about it?
turns.zh: 是的。你看到的是——如果他们现在不买，会不会显得奇怪？他们的行为是不是好像不买才奇怪？有没有那种——你知道，有那种“我会买这个想法”的口头承诺，和他们实际会买的信号。是身体语言吗？你怎么知道他们是认真的？

turns.en: So I call it like a pull-shaped action. Not a good term, but a pull-shaped action is like, 'I need this right now. How do—like I am pulling it out of you. How do we move forward right now?' It is not like, 'Oh, I could totally see us using this in Q4.' That's not pulling towards me. That's kind of pushing out into the future.
turns.zh: 所以我称之为“拉力形状的行动”。不是个好词，但“拉力形状的行动”就像是：“我现在就需要这个。怎么——就像我在从你那里把它拉出来。我们现在怎么推进？”而不是：“哦，我完全能想象我们在第四季度用这个。”那不是把我拉过去，那是推向未来。

turns.en: Like the urgency of like I need those now.
turns.zh: 就像那种“我现在就需要”的紧迫感。

turns.en: There's always this advice of solve your own problem, which is different from what you described. Is that a path you recommend or would you recommend against that?
turns.zh: 总是有“解决你自己的问题”这种建议，这和你描述的不同。这是你推荐的路，还是你会反对？

turns.en: So a friend—um, so like Emily at a company called Clearly AI—she was in security engineering at AWS and she found something there that she would have paid somebody to solve but there was nobody out there. And so in that case it's solve your own problem. Yes, 100%. Where the solve your own problem falls kind of flat a lot of times is it's a thing that you wouldn't have paid somebody to do for you but you just think should exist, right? If it's—and so you have to be honest with yourself. I have done things where I've built things that like, oh, I think the world needs this. I ran into this problem but if I looked myself in the mirror I wouldn't have said yeah buy this right now.
turns.zh: 所以一个朋友——嗯，比如 Clearly AI 公司的 Emily——她之前在 AWS 做安全工程，她在那里发现了一个她愿意付钱请人解决的问题，但外面没有人做。所以那种情况下就是解决你自己的问题。是的，百分之百。而“解决你自己的问题”很多时候效果不佳，是因为那件事你不会付钱请人做，你只是觉得它应该存在，对吧？所以你必须对自己诚实。我做过一些东西，我会想，哦，我觉得世界需要这个。我遇到了这个问题，但如果我照镜子，我不会说“是的，现在就买这个”。

turns.en: Along those lines. Is this advice mostly for B2B SAS sort of software or is this applicable to say consumer app?
turns.zh: 沿着这个思路。这个建议主要是针对 B2B SaaS 类软件，还是也适用于比如消费者应用？

turns.en: So, I am mostly in the B2B space, but I have seen quite a few people—I've been kind of surprised that a lot of people from the consumer space have used this as well. And someone sent me the story of like Spanx, which was basically she did the same thing of selling one-on-one with people, seeing how they reacted to figure out all the different pieces of what became Spanx.
turns.zh: 所以，我主要在 B2B 领域，但我见过不少人——我有点惊讶，很多来自消费者领域的人也用了这个方法。有人发给我 Spanx 的故事，基本上她也是做同样的事，一对一地向人们销售，观察他们的反应，来弄清楚最终成为 Spanx 的各个部分。

turns.en: Yeah. And she solved her own problem famously.
turns.zh: 是的。而且她 famously 解决了自己的问题。

turns.en: Yes. Just tore off her pantyhose. I think that's the story. Just because she needed it now. I think it was like yeah, she's going to event. So that's a cool example.
turns.zh: 是的。就是撕掉了她的连裤袜。我想那是故事。因为她现在就需要。我想是，是的，她要去参加活动。所以那是个很酷的例子。

turns.en: You have this—we're going to talk more about this, but you have this idea of the Hail Mary approach. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 你有这个——我们会多聊这个，但你有这个“万福玛利亚”方法的概念。谈谈那个。

turns.en: So the Hail Mary, so we've been talking about the happy path here. You find something, you're talking with people and they're like, 'Oh my gosh, yeah, this is exactly what I need.' A lot of the time that's not going to happen. You're going to get that kind of lukewarm feel. And so what I've tended to find is that's also an opportunity to what I call throw the Hail Mary, which is okay, this doesn't seem to be a thing. Is there anything on your to-do list that you would pay me to do right now, like that you would pay somebody to take off your plate? And that's just an open-ended Hail Mary. I've actually seen quite a few startups totally pivot and take off from the Hail Mary, which has been really interesting. There's one startup they were trying to sell an applicant tracking system into governments and they had a call with somebody and the person was like, 'Yeah, that's kind of interesting.' But after the Hail Mary question, yeah, what I'd actually pay you to solve is this like job description thing right now. And that became their first contract. That became their first customer and they've grown super fast since then.
turns.zh: 所以“万福玛利亚”，我们一直在说顺利路径。你找到某个东西，你和人们交谈，他们说：“哦天哪，是的，这正是我需要的。”很多时候这不会发生。你会得到那种不温不火的感觉。所以我倾向于发现，这也是一个机会，我称之为“抛出万福玛利亚”，就是：好吧，这似乎不是个事儿。你待办清单上有没有什么你现在愿意付钱让我做的，比如你愿意付钱请人从你盘子里拿走的？那就是一个开放式的万福玛利亚。我实际上见过不少初创公司完全转型并从万福玛利亚中起飞，这真的很有趣。有一家初创公司，他们试图向政府销售申请人跟踪系统，他们和某人通电话，那人说：“是的，有点意思。”但在万福玛利亚问题之后，是的，我实际上愿意付钱让你解决的是这个职位描述的东西，现在就要。那成了他们的第一份合同。那成了他们的第一个客户，从那以后他们增长超快。

turns.en: That's awesome. So the advice here is just sometimes feel free to just ask what problem can we solve for you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以这里的建议就是，有时候不妨直接问：我们能为你解决什么问题？

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And that like leads to how to think about sales. Well, I'll just give a little and we can dig into this if it's interesting, but like I always was kind of nervous to sell as a mega introvert and overthinker. Like it just feels like a lot of pressure. Um, and it like I need to convince you to buy. And so that question feels uncomfortable. But if you kind of reframe it in your own head of I'm just seeing if they need help with anything that they are stuck on. And if they don't, that's fine. But if they do, cool. We can explore if it if I can help. Then uh it kind of changes your orientation towards sales.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。这引出了如何思考销售。好吧，我就简单说一点，如果有趣我们可以深入，但作为一个超级内向和过度思考者，我总是有点害怕销售。就像感觉压力很大。嗯，就像我需要说服你买。所以那个问题感觉不舒服。但如果你在自己脑子里重新框定：我只是看看他们是否需要帮助解决任何卡住的事情。如果他们不需要，那没关系。但如果他们需要，酷。我们可以探索我是否能帮忙。然后这就会改变你对销售的态度。

turns.en: I am in the same boat as you. And that's a really nice way of thinking about it. I'm just trying to solve someone's problem. Why is it so hard? Before we get to the next step, which is getting your first sales call, finding basically finding someone to talk to that you don't already know, are there any anti-patterns or just kind of signals or just like traps people fall into when they're coming up with ideas?
turns.zh: 我和你处境相同。这是很好的思考方式。我只是在试着解决某人的问题。为什么这么难？在我们进入下一步之前，也就是获得你的第一次销售电话，基本上找到你不认识的人交谈，人们在想点子时有没有什么反模式，或者信号，或者陷阱？

turns.en: Yeah, the infinite, but the main ones that I have seen that are like really really brutal are feeling like you need to build it yourself first. So, you come up with an idea and you're like, I don't think this is ready for prime time or I think people have to see it to get it and then you go heads down and build it. Now, now with AI, you can kind of get that out of your system in a hopefully a couple weeks instead of, you know, months or not. But, uh, you do not—you want to face the cold wind of reality as soon as possible. And so don't delay the customer conversations where you can actually find pull.
turns.zh: 是的，无限多，但我见过的主要的、真正残酷的是，觉得自己需要先把它建出来。所以，你想到一个点子，你会想，我觉得这还没准备好或者我觉得人们得看到才能理解，然后你就埋头去建。现在有了 AI，你可以在几周内而不是几个月内把这种冲动释放掉。但是，你不想——你想尽快面对现实的冷风。所以不要推迟那些你能真正找到拉力的客户对话。

turns.en: You're also not a fan of design partners which is okay. Say more because this is typically very standard advice to find design partners.
turns.zh: 你也不喜欢设计合作伙伴，这没问题。多说点，因为找设计合作伙伴通常是标准建议。

turns.en: Yeah. I don't know, maybe in some context it's helpful. I have yet to see it help be helpful.
turns.zh: 是的。我不知道，也许在某些情况下有帮助。我还没见过它有帮助。

turns.en: What I've seen basically every single time I've seen somebody with a design partner is that you recruit a design partner who quote unquote buys into your vision for the product, and they give a bunch of feedback and never buy from you. They never buy, and you realize that all of their feedback was just them playing Steve Jobs, like 'I'm going to help this startup' versus 'I have something I'm actually trying to get done.' And if you think about it, the people who actually have something really important they're trying to get done, they don't want to be a design partner. They just want that thing done.
turns.zh: 我几乎每次看到有人用设计合作伙伴，情况都是：你招募了一个设计合作伙伴，他口头上“认同”你的产品愿景，给了一堆反馈，却从来不买你的产品。他们从不购买，然后你意识到他们所有的反馈都只是在扮演史蒂夫·乔布斯，像是“我要帮帮这家初创公司”，而不是“我有一件真正想完成的事”。你想想，那些真正有重要事情要完成的人，他们不想当设计合作伙伴。他们只想把那件事做成。

turns.en: I love that. Okay. So your advice is don't set up a bunch of design partners, and we'll go through the process you actually recommend. Okay. So, I guess just to think about this coming up with an idea step. The core moment is some insight based on being hands-on living with the people that you will be helping. The term I've heard to describe this idea—I think it was a VC at Floodgate that uses this—you're basically looking for an earned secret. Yes. And your advice here is the way to find an earned secret is either you have lived it at a company, say Amazon gave this AWS example, or you're on the ground working side by side with the people dealing with it and just looking for problems that they have.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个观点。好，所以你的建议是不要设立一堆设计合作伙伴，然后我们会走一遍你真正推荐的流程。好，我想先想想这个“想出点子”的阶段。核心时刻是基于亲身实践、与你要帮助的人共同生活而获得的某种洞察。我听过一个词来描述这个想法——我想是 Floodgate 的一位风投用的——你基本上是在寻找一个“赚来的秘密”。是的。而你的建议是，找到赚来的秘密的方式要么是你在某家公司亲身经历过，比如亚马逊给出的 AWS 例子，要么是你在一线跟处理问题的人并肩工作，寻找他们遇到的问题。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And the method kind of doesn't matter. It might come to you in an IASCA retreat. You could get that secret from anywhere, but the things that are most likely to actually work are getting your hands dirty and learning it from reality versus from theory.
turns.zh: 对，对，对。方法其实不太重要。它可能在一个 IASCA 静修营里降临到你身上。你从任何地方都可能获得那个秘密，但最有可能真正奏效的是亲自动手、从现实中而非理论中学习。

turns.en: So just to follow that thread, say there's like a pie chart of the say 50 companies you've worked with where their idea came from. What would be like the biggest chunks of the pie chart?
turns.zh: 那就顺着这条线说，假设有一个饼图，显示你合作过的比如 50 家公司，他们的点子来自哪里。饼图中最大的几块会是什么？

turns.en: I would say 10% own experience, 90% going and getting firsthand experience. And within that, it's been a bit of some of them sold the wrong product to figure out what the right product was. But most of them actually go and do the thing firsthand.
turns.zh: 我会说 10% 是自身经验，90% 是去获得第一手经验。其中，有些公司是先卖了错误的产品才弄清楚什么是对的产品。但大多数实际上都是亲自去做那件事。

turns.en: And then what percentage IASCA retreat? There's no room for that.
turns.zh: 那 IASCA 静修营占多少百分比？没地方放这个了。

turns.en: 100%. That's mandatory as part of me advising you. That's the pull hypothesis.
turns.zh: 100%。这是我给你建议的强制部分。那就是拉力假设。

turns.en: Okay, sweet. Okay, so say at this point you've got a pull hypothesis. There's signs that maybe there's something really good here. The next phase in my eyes is finding someone to talk to and sell it to. So basically landing a first sales call. Talk about how you go about landing that call and what happens kind of, and then we'll talk about actually running the call. But before we get there, just like finding people to talk to.
turns.zh: 好，太好了。那么假设此时你有了一个拉力假设。有迹象表明这里可能有些非常好的东西。在我看来，下一个阶段是找到可以交谈并销售的人。所以基本上是拿下第一次销售电话。谈谈你如何拿下那个电话以及大概会发生什么，然后我们再谈实际进行电话。但在那之前，先说说找到可以交谈的人。

turns.en: Yeah, this is a fun one. So my goal is actually I want to have two to three conversations per day with potential customers. But to get there, you have to first get your first conversation. So you can do warm intros, you can do all that kind of stuff. We'll just talk about if you don't have any of that and you need to get people to talk to you cold. The way I typically recommend founders start is to just reach out to your potential customers on LinkedIn or via email, and it's with a very specific kind of message that is not a 'hey do you have XYZ pain points, would you like to buy our game-changing solution'—like no template you get online is going to get you any responses except for like 'leave me alone.' And so I call it founder magic kind of outreach at this stage, which is basically like 'you're interesting, I'm interesting. Let's chat and see.' And this is totally acceptable. Like one of the startups that I helped, their message was, 'Hey, Snoop Dogg invested in us and I thought you'd find it interesting too. Would you be open to chat?' That's a fun message. Everyone has their own version of that. Like everyone who listens to this or everyone who's a founder has an interesting message you can send, and you don't have to convince them in the message to buy your product. You just get them to talk with you. This pull exists out there on their to-do list. And so the message doesn't do anything about that. It's just to get them to talk to you. So just say something interesting to cause them to meet with you.
turns.zh: 对，这个有意思。我的目标其实是每天与潜在客户进行两到三次对话。但要做到这一点，你得先获得第一次对话。你可以做暖介绍，所有那些都可以。我们只谈如果你没有任何这些资源，需要冷启动让人们跟你交谈的情况。我通常建议创始人开始的方式是，直接在 LinkedIn 或通过电子邮件联系你的潜在客户，用非常特定的信息，而不是“嘿，你有 XYZ 痛点吗，你想买我们改变游戏规则的解决方案吗”——你在网上找到的任何模板都不会得到任何回复，除了“别烦我”。所以在这个阶段我称之为创始人魔法式外联，基本上就是“你很有趣，我很有趣。我们聊聊看。”这完全可以接受。比如我帮助过的一家初创公司，他们的信息是：“嘿，Snoop Dogg 投资了我们，我想你也会觉得有趣。你愿意聊聊吗？”这是一条有趣的信息。每个人都有自己的版本。就像每个听这个节目的人或每个创始人都有可以发送的有趣信息，你不必在信息中说服他们购买你的产品。你只是让他们和你交谈。这个拉力存在于他们的待办事项清单上。所以信息对此不做任何事。它只是让他们和你交谈。所以就说些有趣的事情，促使他们与你见面。

turns.en: Okay, this is really helpful. So your advice here is don't craft like a whole value prop pitch problem identification. Don't tell them how much pain you're going to solve. It's just like get their attention with something interesting. Yes. The Snoop Dogg example is awesome. Any other examples? Any other kind of ways of thinking about what might be interesting to someone?
turns.zh: 好，这真的很有帮助。所以你的建议是不要精心制作完整的价值主张推销、问题识别。不要告诉他们你将解决多少痛苦。就像用一些有趣的东西引起他们的注意。是的。Snoop Dogg 的例子很棒。还有其他例子吗？还有其他思考什么可能对某人有趣的方式吗？

turns.en: There's been a variety of ones that I've seen. Random ones that are like, 'Hey, I dropped out of my PhD and I'm now working on something for content marketers, right?' Like something that's just kind of interesting enough there that's not super magical. You can have—there's a variety of different things I've seen from 'I was Sam Altman's chief of staff,' right? That, you know, if anybody sends that message, that will work quite well. It doesn't matter what the rest of the message says. 'I thought you'd be interesting and open to chat.' And so, it's finding something interesting that's like worth a conversation with them.
turns.zh: 我见过各种各样的。随机的比如：“嘿，我博士辍学了，现在在为内容营销人员做东西，对吧？”就像某种足够有趣但并非超级神奇的东西。你可以有——我见过各种各样的，从“我曾是 Sam Altman 的幕僚长”，对吧？你知道，如果任何人发送那条信息，那会非常有效。信息其余部分说什么都不重要。“我觉得你会感兴趣，愿意聊聊吗。”所以，就是找到一些有趣的东西，值得与他们对话。

turns.en: Yeah. Like what I'd say is it really depends on your end customer too because if you're doing outreach to like for example HVAC companies saying hey I'm Sam Altman's former chief of staff thought you might find it interesting we're going to say buddy I have no idea what the words in this message mean. So it could be like hey I was at my dad like I worked at my family's plumbing company in in high school and now I'm do working on this kind of uh interesting thing. turns.en: So, say you've landed a call and you're going to do a sales call, say your first one. What is your advice for doing a great job on the on the sales call?
turns.zh: 那么，假设你约到了一个电话，你要做一个销售电话，比如你的第一个。你对在销售电话中做得很好有什么建议？

turns.en: mostly two steps in a sales call. There's the pull discovery step and then there's the kind of conceptual pitch of how we might help step. And so the uh the theory behind a sales call is again it's like if you have pull you're going to rip the thing out of my hands. I don't come into this call like wired up ready to try to convince you to buy like super ant. No, it's just if you have pull, you're going to convince me to let you buy.
turns.zh: 销售电话主要有两个步骤。有拉力发现步骤，然后是我们可能如何帮助的概念性推介步骤。所以销售电话背后的理论再次是，如果你有拉力，你会把东西从我手中抢走。我不会像超级蚂蚁一样， wired up 准备说服你购买。不，只是如果你有拉力，你会说服我让你购买。

turns.en: And so I approach this with the vibe of just like waned back, excited to chat. Let's let's see if I might be able to help you. And so I have a very specific structure of a sales call that I recommend for getting into discovery and then transitioning out of discovery. Basically that you start the call, hey, thanks so much for taking the time. I'm curious. I'm sure you get a bunch of people reaching out to you. like why did you take the call with me today? That's a chance for them to say, you know, you mentioned AI agents and I've been thinking about this and I've just been waiting and I looked at your website. I whatever whatever it winds up being and they they fill out the entire poll framework for you right there. That's ideal. And then you can say, "Oh, that's interesting. Let me can I ask a couple follow-ups?" But most of the time they'll say, "I don't know. You reached out to me. Excited to hear what you have to say." Say, "Great." You use what they have just told you and say, "Okay, great. That sounds like a great agenda for today's call. We can do that. That does that sound good to you?" Get their thumbs up on the agenda. And then you earn the right to ask them some discovery questions about their poll by saying, "Great. Okay, before we get to those items on your, you know, on our agenda, um, do you mind if I ask you a few questions to better understand your context?" And that way you've earned the right to ask questions. it does not feel like an interrogation to them because if it does uh they're not telling you anything.
turns.zh: 所以我以轻松、兴奋交谈的氛围来处理这件事。让我们看看我是否能帮到你。所以我有一个非常具体的销售电话结构，我推荐用于进入发现阶段然后过渡出发现阶段。基本上，你开始电话时说：“嘿，非常感谢你抽出时间。我很好奇。我确定有很多人联系你。你为什么今天接我的电话？”这是让他们说：“你知道，你提到了 AI 智能体，我一直在思考这个，我一直在等待，我看了你的网站。”不管是什么，他们就在那里为你填写了整个拉力框架。那很理想。然后你可以说：“哦，那很有趣。让我——我可以问几个后续问题吗？”但大多数时候他们会说：“我不知道。你联系了我。很兴奋听到你要说什么。”说：“太好了。”你利用他们刚刚告诉你的话，说：“好的，太好了。这听起来像是今天电话的好议程。我们可以这样做。那听起来对你合适吗？”得到他们对议程的认可。然后你通过说：“太好了。好的，在我们讨论你议程上的那些项目之前，嗯，你介意我问你几个问题来更好地了解你的背景吗？”来赢得问他们关于拉力的发现问题的权利。这样你就赢得了提问的权利。这对他们来说不像是审讯，因为如果是的话，他们什么都不会告诉你。

turns.en: Okay, a few tactical questions. One is just how long should you try to make this call? How long should your invite be for? And then where does where does a demo fit in? Do you recommend demo on this call or doing a separate call for that?

ts.sec: Selling to Learn, Not to Push

turns.en: I imagine a lot of founders are just so excited and convinced this is real, and your approach is just, here's a way to validate that and be really real with what's working or not.
turns.zh: 我猜很多创始人都会特别兴奋、坚信这是真的，而你的方法就是：这里有一种方式去验证它，并且非常真实地面对什么有效、什么无效。

turns.en: Yeah. I think it's thinking of it as we're selling to learn, not really to push something. Not to push. We're going to learn and we're seeing if they try to buy. If they don't, cool. We've learned something. We can keep iterating from there. If they do, okay, great. Now we might have something. Let's see if it repeats.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得就是把它想成：我们销售是为了学习，而不是真的要推什么东西。不是去推。我们要去学习，看看他们会不会尝试购买。如果不会，很好，我们学到了东西，可以继续迭代。如果会，好，太棒了，也许我们真有点东西了，看看它会不会重复出现。

turns.en: The whole idea of calling this pull is so smart, because you always hear product-market fit is you're feeling pull. You're feeling pulled. This boulder is pulling you down. The wind is pushing you.

ts.sec: What a Good Sales Call Looks Like

turns.en: Is there an example that comes to mind when you think about a good sales call, what that kind of feels like, looks like, what a pitch would be?
turns.zh: 当你想到一场好的销售电话时，有没有什么例子？那种感觉、那种样子、那种推销会是什么样的？

turns.en: Yeah. So what you're trying to do is you're trying to get again the pull out of them. And so they say, I'm trying to make a website, but one of those typical point-and-click website design things are just too much effort for me, right? So you have something about pull there. You've kind of pulled that out of them. They've described that. And so the kind of interesting thing is that once you have pull, your pitch is quite simple. What you're not trying to do here is you're not trying to describe this massive product vision or your theory of the problem. You know that they're trying to do X but blocked because of Y. And so your pitch in that case is, okay, so it sounds like you're looking for something to make a website without all the hassle of a point-and-click thing. Is that roughly it? And you describe it in a really small and simple way. Not a really big way. You describe it in a small way and they say, yeah, that sounds like it. How exactly does that work? Tell me more. They're pulling more information out of you, and that's when you know you're starting to be on to something.
turns.zh: 对。你要做的是再次从他们身上引出拉力。比如他们说，我想做个网站，但那种典型的点击式网站设计工具对我来说太费劲了，对吧？那你就有一点拉力了。你算是把它从他们身上引出来了，他们描述了这一点。有意思的是，一旦你有了拉力，你的推销就很简单。你在这里不是要描述一个宏大的产品愿景，也不是要讲你对问题的理论。你知道他们想做 X，但因为 Y 被卡住了。所以这种情况下你的推销就是：好，听起来你在找一个能让你做网站、又不用忍受点击式工具那些麻烦的东西，大致是这样吗？你用非常非常小、非常简单的方式去描述，而不是用很大的方式。你用小方式描述，他们说，对，听起来是这样。那它到底怎么运作？多跟我说说。他们在从你身上拉出更多信息，这时候你就知道自己开始摸到门道了。

turns.en: And are you in your head thinking through the pull framework of these four points and just thinking through like, okay, is this actually something they need right now and unavoidable? Are there, what are their alternatives? And kind of thinking through all that?
turns.zh: 你会在脑子里过一遍那个拉力框架的四个要点吗？就是想着：好，这真的是他们现在需要、而且不可避免的事吗？他们的替代方案是什么？把所有这些都过一遍？

ts.sec: The Status Quo and the Bar to Switch

turns.en: So this touches on a like we haven't actually addressed the specific challenge, which is that there's a lot you have to get over for people to decide to try something new and to buy something new. The status quo is generally fine. They have so many priorities. They have so many things they're dealing with. Just like the bar to get over for people to be like, I want this. I'm going to buy it now is really high. And the idea here of this framework is to get over that hump.
turns.zh: 这触及到一个我们其实还没谈到的具体挑战：要让人决定尝试新东西、购买新东西，你得跨过很多障碍。现状通常还行。他们有那么多优先事项，有那么多事要处理。要让人说“我想要这个，我现在就买”，这个门槛真的很高。而这个框架的想法就是跨过那道坎。

turns.en: Well, it's to find the people for whom the status quo is not okay, right? It's to find the people, you know, everyone says like change is hard and all this kind of stuff. Well, you're looking for the people who are already trying to change, who don't need convincing.
turns.zh: 嗯，它是去找那些现状对他们来说不行的人，对吧？是去找那些人。你知道，大家都说改变很难之类的。你要找的是那些已经在尝试改变、不需要被说服的人。

ts.sec: How Much Better Does It Have to Be?

turns.en: There's this idea that your product has to be 10 times better than the existing solution for anyone to care. Do you feel like, how do you think about, okay, this is better, they tried alternatives, none of them do it, or some of them do it. Okay, like how much better does this have to be for them to care? Or is it okay if it's just, you know, just a little bit better?
turns.zh: 有一种说法是，你的产品必须比现有方案好 10 倍，才会有人在意。你觉得，你怎么看：好，这个更好，他们试过替代方案，没有一个能做到，或者有些能做到。那它得好多少，他们才会在意？还是说，只要好一点点也可以？

turns.en: The example with Jump, I think again the AI note-taker for financial advisors is a good one. How much better are they than the other generic AI note-takers? Well, if those note-takers don't get the job done and we do, they are infinitely better. They unblock something. And so that's kind of how I think about how stuck are they with their existing options. And so I don't know, I don't know about 10x. Like, that thing doesn't quite register in my head. It's really, are they a coiled spring, and how do they respond when I show up?
turns.zh: Jump 那个例子，我觉得那个面向财务顾问的 AI 笔记工具就是个好例子。它们比其他通用的 AI 笔记工具好多少？如果那些笔记工具干不成这活，而我们能干成，那它们就是无限好。它们解开了一个卡点。所以这就是我思考他们被现有方案卡得有多死的方式。所以我不知道，我不太确定 10 倍这个说法。那个东西在我脑子里不太成立。真正的问题是：他们是不是一根压紧的弹簧？当我出现时，他们怎么反应？

turns.en: So I think about a company like Linear who competes with Jira. I don't know if you know, do you know Linear?
turns.zh: 我会想到像 Linear 这样跟 Jira 竞争的公司。我不知道你知不知道，你了解 Linear 吗？

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 知道。知道。知道。

turns.en: So just, I'm curious if it applies through this framework. So in my understanding, Linear wins over Jira often because the experience is just better. It's just like a beautiful, smooth, well-crafted experience. And so they win a lot of customers because it just feels nice and engineers really like using it.
turns.zh: 我就是好奇，这能不能套进这个框架。据我理解，Linear 常常能赢过 Jira，就是因为体验就是更好。就是一种漂亮、顺滑、精心打磨的体验。所以他们赢了很多客户，因为用起来就是舒服，工程师真的很喜欢用它。

turns.en: Do you feel like that works through the pull framework or is there something else going on there?
turns.zh: 你觉得这是通过拉力框架起作用的，还是有其他因素？

turns.en: Again, if we use the pull framework to analyze that situation, what would have to be true is there's a certain kind of person who is trying to do their issue tracking, but they are blocked from doing something around issue tracking and something about Jira's experience is blocking them from doing it the way such that Linear's way better experience is actually relevant to them. Right? I've made the mistake of taking that analogy and being like, 'Okay, so I can just come into a category with way better UX, way better experience, and I'm going to crush it.' And I tried that in HR software and it turned out the user experience was not relevant to the buyer and so they didn't care that their systems look like they're still on Cobalt or whatever it is. So it wasn't relevant there. But again, the pull theory would say that in the case of Jira versus Linear, there was a kind of person who was blocked by Jira's experience. And I imagine the stronger the pull, the faster all this stuff happens. It grows. I know Linear took a long time to get people using it, to trust it, to switch. And so maybe the pull wasn't as strong because there wasn't as much of that blocking, and it was more of just like, 'Okay, I can just move faster, be happier.' It took longer. Do you find that the stronger the pull, the faster the company grows?
turns.zh: 再次，如果我们用拉力框架来分析那种情况，那么必须成立的是：有某类人正在尝试进行问题跟踪，但他们在问题跟踪方面遇到了阻碍，而 Jira 的体验在某些方面阻止了他们以某种方式去做，使得 Linear 更好的体验对他们来说真正相关。对吧？我犯过这样的错误：把这个类比拿过来，然后说：‘好吧，那我就可以进入一个品类，用更好的用户体验、更好的体验，然后我会碾压它。’我在 HR 软件上试过，结果发现用户体验与买家无关，所以他们不在乎他们的系统看起来还停留在 Cobalt 时代什么的。所以在那里并不相关。但再次，拉力理论会说，在 Jira 与 Linear 的案例中，有某类人被 Jira 的体验所阻碍。我想拉力越强，所有这些事情发生得就越快。它增长得越快。我知道 Linear 花了很长时间才让人们使用它、信任它、切换过来。所以也许拉力没有那么强，因为没有那么多阻碍，而更多只是‘好吧，我可以更快地行动，更开心。’它花了更长时间。你是否发现拉力越强，公司增长得越快？

turns.en: Yeah, I've seen a bunch of startups where they go zero to whatever, like everyone now is going zero to infinity super fast, and it's because they have found these pockets of pull where people will rip a product out of their hands. And people will see these AI pitches now and it's like, 'Wait a second, it can do X,' and buy basically instantly. And I've seen that happen in enterprise. I saw an enterprise deal close in like two weeks and it's just like that thing did. When I was growing up, enterprise deals took 18 months. Like what the heck?
turns.zh: 是的，我见过很多初创公司从零到 whatever，就像现在每个人都在从零到无限，超级快，这是因为他们找到了这些拉力口袋，人们会从他们手中抢走产品。现在人们看到这些 AI 推销，就会说：‘等一下，它能做 X，’然后基本上立刻购买。我见过这种情况在企业中发生。我见过一笔企业交易在两周内完成，就像那件事一样。在我成长的过程中，企业交易需要 18 个月。搞什么鬼？

turns.en: Okay, so let's move on to the next step. So, at this point, you had your first sales call. I imagine the next step is closing the deal. And I'm interested because it's still early. You may not even have a product. What does that look like going from, 'Okay, I want to buy it now.' What do you do next?
turns.zh: 好的，那么让我们进入下一步。此时，你已经进行了第一次销售电话。我想下一步是完成交易。我感兴趣是因为这还很早。你可能甚至还没有产品。从‘好的，我现在想买它’到下一步，那是什么样子的？你接下来做什么？

turns.en: Yeah. So, it's going to depend on the size of the deal, but you want to come back with some sort of a concept and some sort of a plan. And so, examples of this: the pharma company that I mentioned earlier, the company selling into pharma, he showed up and just threw a Hail Mary on an intro to a pharma exec. Pharma exec was like, 'Oh my gosh, thank you so much for asking. Our current market research is da da da da. We're trying. It's just so bad. It's so slow.' And the founder was like, 'Okay, I don't even have slides here. I'm just hearing this for the first time.' And so it sounds like you're looking for faster market research that looks like the current research you're getting but kind of, I don't know, like it's just better in these kinds of ways. Is that roughly right? And the exec was like, 'Yes, that's exactly it.' And so the founder is like, 'Okay, let's do this. What if I come back to you in a couple days with a kind of mockup of what I think that could look like and then we can discuss if that fits what you're really looking for and then decide if we want to move forward.' And so in that case, no slides, no nothing. Goes and vibe codes a kind of rough layout of what this would look like, gets some feedback on it, says, 'Okay, based on that, is there anything else you need to know to decide whether this is a fit that you want to bring into your organization?' Says, 'Yeah, what's the price?' And then there's a talk track you can use for price, but that's basically it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，这取决于交易规模，但你需要带着某种概念和某种计划回来。举个例子：我之前提到的制药公司，那家向制药公司销售的公司，他出现后，在介绍给制药高管时孤注一掷。制药高管说：‘哦天哪，非常感谢你问这个问题。我们目前的市场研究是哒哒哒哒。我们正在尝试。它太糟糕了。太慢了。’创始人说：‘好的，我甚至没有幻灯片，我是第一次听到这个。’所以听起来你在寻找更快的市场研究，看起来像你目前得到的研究，但有点，我不知道，就像在这些方面更好。大致对吗？高管说：‘是的，正是如此。’创始人说：‘好的，我们这样做吧。如果我几天后回来给你一个我认为可能是什么样子的模型，然后我们可以讨论这是否符合你真正想要的，然后决定我们是否想继续推进。’所以在这种情况下，没有幻灯片，什么都没有。去 vibe code 一个粗略的布局，得到一些反馈，说：‘好的，基于这个，你还需要知道什么来决定这是否是你想引入组织的合适选择？’说：‘是的，价格是多少？’然后有一个你可以用于价格的谈话轨道，但基本上就是这样。

turns.en: Okay. Tell me more about this price talk track.
turns.zh: 好的。多告诉我一些关于这个价格谈话轨道的事情。

turns.en: Yeah. So the interesting thing about the pull framework is that it can help you set the bounds for pricing. So what's the value of getting the project done or what are the costs of the alternatives? So the L's, so what's the value of getting this market research faster or what is the cost you're currently spending with your market research consultants? Both of those can tell you, 'Okay, the value of market research is like X. The cost with consultants is, I don't know, $50,000 per year.' And so that gives me a rough boundary to say, 'Okay, what if we charged $50,000 a year, the same price as your current market research consultants?' It gives a frame on price that makes it intuitive to your potential customers.
turns.zh: 是的。所以拉力框架的有趣之处在于它可以帮助你设定定价的边界。那么完成项目的价值是什么，或者替代方案的成本是什么？所以 L 的，那么更快获得市场研究的价值是什么，或者你目前花在市场研究顾问上的成本是多少？两者都可以告诉你：‘好的，市场研究的价值大约是 X。顾问的成本是，我不知道，每年 5 万美元。’所以这给了我一个粗略的边界来说：‘好的，如果我们每年收费 5 万美元，和你目前的市场研究顾问价格一样呢？’它提供了一个价格框架，让你的潜在客户觉得直观。

turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So the way you've written about this closing step, there's kind of two parts. There's the fit of just like is this a fit and then it's just a bunch of project management to get the deal closed. So we've spent a lot of time I think on the fit. The project management, is there anything there important to talk about?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。所以你写到的这个成交步骤，大致有两个部分。一个是契合度，就是这是否合适，然后就是一堆项目管理来让交易完成。所以我认为我们已经花了很多时间在契合度上。项目管理方面，有什么重要的要谈吗？

turns.en: Yeah. So this is, you did a great episode with Jen, a great couple episodes with Jen on the sales process. And so in bigger deals, enterprise deals, there's like the champion has pull and decides, 'Yes, I want this.' And then you have to do a set of like 17 demos. You have to genuflect in front of four committees. Like there's all of these things that you have to do. For smaller deals, you don't have to do that kind of stuff. It might just be the CEO who's like, 'Yeah, cool. Next step is you send me the Stripe link and we schedule an onboarding call.' And so the project management step will depend. My typical recommendation for project management in larger organizations is to have a conversation with the buyer, with the champion, to say, 'Okay, cool, this is the project on your to-do list. When does this need to be showing results by?' They'll say, 'Oh, definitely Q1 next year.' 'Okay, cool, that's a forcing function.' You work backwards from there to say, 'Okay, given that we need to be live Q1, what are the set of steps that need to happen between now and then so we can be deployed and showing results by then?' And that is a forcing function for all of the pro steps in the sales process.
turns.zh: 是的。所以这是，你和 Jen 做了一期很棒的节目，和 Jen 做了几期很棒的关于销售流程的节目。所以在更大的交易中，企业交易中，冠军有拉力并决定‘是的，我想要这个。’然后你必须做一系列大约 17 个演示。你必须在四个委员会面前卑躬屈膝。就像你必须做所有这些事情。对于较小的交易，你不需要做那种事情。可能只是 CEO 说：‘是的，酷。下一步是你给我发 Stripe 链接，我们安排一次入职电话。’所以项目管理步骤将取决于情况。我通常对大型组织中的项目管理的建议是与买家、与冠军进行对话，说：‘好的，酷，这是你待办事项清单上的项目。这需要在什么时候展示结果？’他们会说：‘哦，肯定是明年第一季度。’‘好的，酷，那是一个强制函数。’你从那里倒推，说：‘好的，鉴于我们需要在第一季度上线，从现在到那时需要发生哪些步骤，以便我们能够部署并在那时展示结果？’这是销售过程中所有专业步骤的强制函数。

turns.en: Awesome. So basically asking when do we need to show success for this to be a thing that you all roll out and then working backwards from that. Okay. At this point a lot of people would create basically design partnership arrangements where they're like, 'Okay cool, we'll build this with you. We'll figure it out as we go. We won't charge you.' Per your earlier point, you were not into design partnerships. I imagine your advice here is just like sell it directly.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以基本上就是问我们什么时候需要展示成功，以便你们全面推出，然后从那里倒推。好的。此时很多人会创建基本上设计合作伙伴的安排，他们会说：‘好的酷，我们会和你一起构建这个。我们会边做边想。我们不会收费。’根据你之前的观点，你不喜欢设计合作伙伴。我想你这里的建议就是直接销售。

turns.en: Don't try to give them to for free. Don't set up some kind of partnership thing.
turns.zh: 不要试图免费给他们。不要建立某种合作关系。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Why? Well, why shoot yourself in the foot?
turns.zh: 是的。是的。为什么？嗯，为什么要自毁前程呢？

turns.en: And again, the reason not to is because it just you find that doesn't lead to the best to stuff that actually sells and works. Building this kind of design partnership relationship.
turns.zh: 再说一次，不这样做的原因是，你会发现这不会带来最好的、真正能卖出去并起作用的东西。建立这种设计合作关系。

turns.en: Yeah. If they're like it it basically takes something from I need to to solve this right now to like okay now I'm helping you build your product. like where what are we doing here? So it it's a negative signal to the most to people with who actually have pole and it's a positive signal to people who don't.
turns.zh: 是的。如果他们像这样，它基本上把一些东西从“我现在需要解决这个问题”变成“好吧，现在我在帮你构建你的产品”。就像，我们在这里做什么？所以这对大多数真正有需求的人来说是一个负面信号，而对没有需求的人来说是一个正面信号。

turns.en: Awesome. Okay, that totally makes sense. Like if there's pull just go with it, you need to Yeah.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，这完全说得通。就像如果有需求，就顺势而为，你需要是的。

turns.en: Yeah. And you can sell something that's like, you know, you might not have a full platform ready. You can sell something that's more service-shaped early on. I've seen a bunch of startups do that where they sell, you know, okay, we're going to have an AI product manager who can do XYZ kind of thing. For now, it's delivered by us while this thing is working behind the scenes. And so you can kind of frame it so they're not expecting a full platform that like enterprise-grade platform ready next week. They expect something more service-shaped and you kind of validate that there's real pull there and you figure out what the actual thing to build is. while delivering it a mix of manually and automated.
turns.zh: 是的。你可以卖一些东西，比如，你知道，你可能还没有一个完整的平台准备好。你可以在早期卖一些更服务形态的东西。我见过很多初创公司这样做，他们卖，你知道，好吧，我们将有一个 AI 产品经理，可以做 XYZ 之类的事情。目前，它由我们提供，而这个东西在幕后工作。所以你可以这样构建，让他们不期待一个完整的平台，比如企业级平台下周就准备好。他们期待的是更服务形态的东西，你验证那里有真正的需求，并弄清楚实际要构建什么。同时以手动和自动的混合方式交付。

turns.en: Okay, that's really interesting. That's come up a lot on the podcast, especially with go to market sales conversations. This idea of services being a great place to start, which historically has been a terrible idea because uh the fear is you never actually get to a place where you can automate it and you're just running a consulting business forever with terrible margins. So, you've seen this work, this idea of starting with basically like humans doing the thing and then slowly building a product around it that increases margins.
turns.zh: 好的，这真的很有趣。这在播客中经常出现，尤其是在市场推广销售对话中。服务是一个很好的起点，这个想法历史上一直是个糟糕的主意，因为呃，担心的是你永远无法真正达到可以自动化的地步，你只是永远经营一家利润率糟糕的咨询公司。所以，你见过这种方法奏效，这个想法基本上是从人工做事情开始，然后慢慢围绕它构建产品来提高利润率。

turns.en: Yeah, it definitely has downsides, right? You definitely can get stuck in a kind of service businesses kind of thing, but everything has downsides.
turns.zh: 是的，它肯定有缺点，对吧？你肯定可能会陷入一种服务业务之类的事情，但一切都有缺点。

turns.en: Awesome. Yeah. And the idea is AI kind of does more and more of this stuff. And part of it is you learn more and more of what uh what the problem opportunities are and things like that with people doing the work. Okay. Um going back to price real quick. Uh classically founders are afraid to ask for big numbers and throw out, you know, high prices. uh knowing that the stuff changes and you'll learn as you go. Any advice for that first price pitch of what number to throw out?
turns.zh: 太棒了。是的。这个想法是 AI 会越来越多地做这些事情。部分原因是，随着人们做这些工作，你会越来越多地了解问题机会是什么等等。好的。嗯，快速回到价格问题。呃，传统上创始人害怕要求大数字并抛出，你知道，高价。呃，知道事情会变化，你会边做边学。对于第一次价格推销，有什么建议，应该抛出什么数字？

turns.en: Yeah. So early on I'm really more testing willingness to transact versus willingness to pay. And so I don't care about pricing a ton in the early couple of customers. That said, I was just working with a company that's their first deal is enterprise and they've got a big demo day coming up and so they're like, "How do we get the most possible revenue out of this so we can look like that for demo day?" Totally valid thing to do. In that case, what you do is you throw out a number in a way that doesn't like get you slapped. And the specific approach that I'd recommend for that is um almost like using a case study as a hey react to this kind of case study. And so you'd say yeah when we talk to others the way they everyone's kind of done pricing differently. Some of them have been you know it's been sometimes it's been a small project for 80,000 other times it's been up to a million in terms of right and these are kind of the levers here and some people a lot of people wind up in the middle. You tell me how are you thinking about this? And so what you're doing is you're not like me on this side proposing pricing to you on this side. It's both of us looking at like an example, a kind of semi-real example of what you've heard from others as how they think about this and letting them them throw up on that. Throw up on that. I like that.

consensus.en: Pull is a property of a person, not a company; sell to the specific individual with a project.
consensus.zh: 拉力是个人属性，而非公司属性；向有具体项目的特定个体销售。

consensus.en: The pull framework: a person has a Project, finds it Unavoidable now, has List of options, and Limitations make them inadequate.
consensus.zh: 拉力框架：一个人有项目（Project），认为现在不可避免（Unavoidable），有选项列表（List），但局限性（Limitations）使现有选项不够好。

consensus.en: If pull exists, the customer will try to buy immediately; otherwise, they won't, and you should move on.
consensus.zh: 如果存在拉力，客户会立即尝试购买；否则不会，你应该继续寻找。

consensus.en: Use the pull hypothesis to test ideas: show it to potential customers and see if they try to buy.
consensus.zh: 用拉力假设测试想法：向潜在客户展示，看他们是否尝试购买。

consensus.en: Retention is critical; design onboarding to reach the leading indicator of retention (X) where churn becomes weird.
consensus.zh: 留存至关重要；设计入职流程以达到留存的领先指标（X），使流失变得奇怪。

consensus.en: Build a case study factory: repeat one case study where customers say 'hell yes' before and after buying.
consensus.zh: 构建案例研究工厂：重复一个客户在购买前后都说“ hell yes”的案例研究。

contrarian.en: Don't build first; face the cold wind of reality as soon as possible by talking to customers.
contrarian.zh: 不要先构建；尽快面对现实的冷风，与客户交谈。

contrarian.en: Avoid design partners; they give feedback but rarely buy, and signal lack of pull.
contrarian.zh: 避免设计合作伙伴；他们提供反馈但很少购买，并表明缺乏拉力。

contrarian.en: Don't offer pilots or proof of concepts proactively; sell directly and roll out.
contrarian.zh: 不要主动提供试点或概念验证；直接销售并推出。

contrarian.en: Cold outreach should be interesting, not value-prop pitches; AI personalization often fails.
contrarian.zh: 冷 outreach 应该有趣，而不是价值主张推销；AI 个性化常常失败。

contrarian.en: Pricing early is about testing willingness to transact, not maximizing revenue.
contrarian.zh: 早期定价是测试交易意愿，而不是最大化收入。

contrarian.en: Don't enter a space with a clear winner without a theory of being different; better UX alone isn't enough.
contrarian.zh: 不要在没有差异化理论的情况下进入已有明显赢家的领域；仅更好的用户体验是不够的。
